history.heading: Dutch and French
paragraphs: Mauritius, a volcanic island in the Indian Ocean east of Madagascar, was uninhabited when Arab and later Portuguese sailors visited. The Dutch settled in 1638 and named it after Prince Maurice of Nassau; the dodo, a flightless bird found only there, was driven to extinction by the late 17th century.
The French took control in 1715, naming it Île de France, and developed sugar plantations worked by enslaved people from Madagascar and Africa.

history.heading: British rule and independence
paragraphs: Britain captured the island in 1810. After slavery was abolished in 1835, about half a million indentured labourers were brought from India, landing at the Aapravasi Ghat, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Their descendants became the majority of the population.

Mauritius became independent on 12 March 1968 under Seewoosagur Ramgoolam and a republic in 1992. Britain detached the Chagos Islands before independence; in 2025 the UK agreed to transfer sovereignty to Mauritius.

culture.heading: A rainbow nation
paragraphs: About two-thirds of Mauritians are of Indian descent, with Creole, Chinese and Franco-Mauritian communities. English is the official language of parliament, while French is widely used and Mauritian Creole is spoken by almost everyone. Hinduism is the largest religion, followed by Christianity and Islam.
Sega, a music and dance with African roots, is recognised by UNESCO. Cuisine includes dholl puri, curries, rougaille and biryani.

politics.heading: Parliamentary democracy
paragraphs: Mauritius is a parliamentary republic and one of Africa's most stable democracies. The prime minister leads the government. Politics has long been dominated by a few families and parties. In the 2024 election, the opposition alliance won all the elected seats, and Navin Ramgoolam returned as prime minister.

economy.heading: An African success story
paragraphs: Mauritius transformed from a sugar-dependent economy into one of Africa's richest countries. Today its economy rests on tourism, textiles, financial services (including offshore finance), information technology and sugar.
The currency is the Mauritian rupee. Challenges include an ageing population and dependence on tourism.
